```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(data.table)
library(here)

# Load scalars produced by estimation scripts.
# Run order: estimate-sumstats-nfip.R, estimate-mhs.R, estimate-nfip.R,
#            then estimate-welfare.R (depends on the other two).
mhs_sc  <- fread(here("output", "results", "mhs-scalars.csv"))
nfip_sc <- fread(here("output", "results", "nfip-scalars.csv"))
welf_sc <- fread(here("output", "results", "welfare-scalars.csv"))
ss_sc   <- fread(here("output", "results", "sumstats-nfip-scalars.csv"))

get_mhs  <- function(nm) mhs_sc[statistic == nm,  value]
get_nfip <- function(nm) nfip_sc[statistic == nm, value]
get_welf <- function(nm) welf_sc[statistic == nm, value]
get_ss   <- function(nm) ss_sc[statistic == nm,   value]

# Formatting helpers.  All monetary values stored in $000 (2000 dollars).
fmt_d <- function(x, digits = 0) {
    paste0("\\$", formatC(abs(round(x * 1000)), format = "f",
                          digits = digits, big.mark = ","))
}
fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 0) {
    paste0(formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits), "%")
}

# Pre-compute formatted values used repeatedly in the text
price_eff      <- fmt_d(get_mhs("price_effect_level"))
price_pct      <- fmt_pct(get_mhs("price_effect_pct"))
avg_price_tr   <- fmt_d(get_mhs("avg_price_treated_pre"))
# Headline ATT: static post_mh coefficient (single precisely-estimated
# number), not the average of the event study's eleven noisy period_constr
# x mh coefficients. The event study (bldg_dmg_evt_avg) is retained for
# describing pre-trends and the post-1994 ramp, not as the headline figure.
bldg_dmg_eff   <- fmt_d(abs(get_nfip("building_damage_static")))
bldg_dmg_se    <- fmt_d(abs(get_nfip("building_damage_static_se")))
bldg_dmg_evt_avg <- fmt_d(abs(get_nfip("building_damage_avg")))
# Damage-share outcome is 100 x damage / assessed value, so coefficients are
# percentage-point changes in that ratio.  Report the static estimate for the
# same reason as building damage: the event-study share coefficients range
# from -22 to +0.8 and a "between X and Y" summary would misrepresent them.
bldg_shr_static    <- formatC(abs(get_nfip("building_damage_share_static")),
                              format = "f", digits = 1)
bldg_shr_static_se <- formatC(abs(get_nfip("building_damage_share_static_se")),
                              format = "f", digits = 1)
cont_dmg_eff   <- fmt_d(abs(get_nfip("contents_damage_avg")))
net_cont_eff   <- fmt_d(abs(get_nfip("net_contents_pmt_avg")))
net_bldg_eff   <- fmt_d(abs(get_nfip("net_building_pmt_avg")))
bldg_pct_avg   <- round(abs(get_nfip("building_damage_avg")) /
                         get_nfip("avg_building_damage_all") * 100)
claim_rate_fmt <- fmt_pct(get_welf("claim_rate_pooled_pre") * 100, 1)
ann_benefit    <- fmt_d(get_welf("annual_benefit"))
npv_baseline   <- fmt_d(get_welf("npv_3pct_20yr"))
bcr_pct        <- fmt_pct(get_welf("bcr_3pct_20yr") * 100)
cost_fmt       <- fmt_d(get_welf("compliance_cost"))
delta_bldg     <- fmt_d(get_welf("delta_building"))
delta_cont     <- fmt_d(get_welf("delta_contents"))
delta_total    <- fmt_d(get_welf("delta_total"))
n_post_claims  <- format(as.integer(get_welf("post_claims_n")), big.mark = ",")
nfip_sav_m     <- paste0("$", round(get_welf("nfip_savings_total") / 1000),
                          " million")
n_mh_claims    <- format(as.integer(get_ss("total_claims_mh")), big.mark = ",")
mh_claim_pct   <- round(get_ss("mh_claim_share") * 100, 1)

# Take-up per housing-unit stock (Chunk E). OLS coefficients on
# policies_per_1k_homes / claims_per_1k_homes (homes_n-weighted, clustered
# by county) are already LEVEL differences per 1,000 homes; report signed
# (direction matters here).
signed_fmt <- function(x, digits = 1) {
    paste0(if (x >= 0) "+" else "-",
           formatC(abs(round(x, digits)), format = "f", digits = digits))
}
ppl_home_per1k <- signed_fmt(get_nfip("policies_per_1k_homes_avg"), 1)
clm_home_per1k <- signed_fmt(get_nfip("claims_per_1k_homes_avg"), 2)
```

\begin{abstract}
Does mandated climate adaptation pay for itself? I study the 1994 HUD wind standard reform, which required structural upgrades to manufactured homes in hurricane-prone areas. Using claim and policy data from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), I compare flood damage to manufactured and site-built homes of different construction vintages exposed to floods in the same county and over the same period. Manufactured homes built after 1994 experience `r bldg_dmg_eff` lower building damage per claim relative to site-built homes of the same vintage. On the cost side, the reform raised manufactured home prices by `r price_eff` in treated states. A back-of-envelope calculation suggests the insured flood channel alone recovers roughly `r bcr_pct` of the upfront cost; the total return---including wind damage, uninsured losses, and reduced risk---is likely higher, but this paper does not measure those channels. For the 22 million Americans living in manufactured homes, many of whom are low-income and lack disaster insurance, the HUD standard functions as built-in catastrophe insurance: it reduces risk automatically, without requiring annual premium payments, claims filing, or compliance with eligibility rules that many manufactured homeowners cannot meet.
\end{abstract}

# Introduction

The U.S. experienced over 100 billion-dollar climate disasters over the five years before 2026, incurring damages of over \$600 billion dollars.[^billion-dollar] These costs are projected to grow substantially as climate change intensifies extreme weather events. Building codes and other forms of mandated adaptation investment are a potential policy tool for reducing disaster losses and risk, but the returns to these investments are not well understood, and they may have indirect effects on household's exposure to climate risk by interacting with insurance markets. This paper provides new evidence on the costs and benefits of mandated adaptation in the context of manufactured housing (MH), a sector that is both highly vulnerable to climate risk and largely -- though not entirely -- uninsured.[^mh]

[^billion-dollar]: Climate Central. "U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters." ClimateCentral.Org, 2026. \href{https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters/summary-stats}{https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters/summary-stats}.

[^mh]: "Manufactured homes" are the preferred industry term and refer specifically to mobile homes that satisfy the 1976 HUD Code. As the vast majority of mobile homes produced since 1976 satisfy the code, I use the terms "manufactured" and "mobile" interchangeably.

Government mandates for costly adaptation may be justified if private take-up is hindered by frictions. For instance, households may misperceive climate risk [@bakkensen_going_2022; @gallagher_learning_2014]. They may fail to internalize benefits to their neighbors [@baylis_mandated_2021]. They may enjoy limited upside from adaptation if mitigation behaviors are not reflected in insurance premiums [@wagner_adaptation_2022]. Finally, they may rely on public insurance programs and disaster relief instead [@deryugina_fiscal_2017; @baylis_moral_2019].

I estimate both the direct cost of compliance, in the form of additional construction costs; and the direct benefits, in reduced flood damage. My results indicate that benefits from the single channel of flood damage reduction do not outweigh the considerable cost of the reform. However, it is possible that accounting for other benefits, such as the insurance value and non-flooding damages, would yield a positive private benefit-cost ratio.

On the cost side, I use the Census Bureau's Manufactured Housing Survey to estimate a difference-in-differences comparing manufactured home prices in states with HUD wind zones II and III (treated) to zone I states (control), before and after 1994. Prices in treated states rose by `r price_eff`, an increase of roughly `r price_pct` on an average of `r avg_price_tr` in treated states. There is no detectable effect on placements, though point estimates are imprecise. Taking the point estimates at face value, a price increase with no change in quantity is consistent with a world where households value the HUD-mandated improvements roughly at cost.

On the benefit side, I use flood insurance claim and policy data from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) to estimate the effect of the HUD standard on flood damage. My identification strategy exploits two sources of variation: MH versus site-built housing, and post-1994 versus pre-1994 construction vintage. County by flood-loss-period fixed effects ensure comparisons are made only between homes exposed to the same floods in the same location. This is a double-difference in vintage and housing type: the site-built comparison group absorbs secular changes in construction quality and storm severity, isolating the manufactured-home-specific break at 1994.

Post-1994 manufactured homes experience `r bldg_dmg_eff` lower building damage per claim relative to pre-1994 manufactured homes, compared to the same vintage difference for site-built homes. The event study shows flat pre-trends and a sharp break at 1994 that grows slightly with later construction cohorts, consistent with delays between the manufacture and installation of MH. I also find that damage as a share of the building's assessed value declines by approximately `r bldg_shr_static` percentage points and that contents payments decline by about `r net_cont_eff` per claim. At the same time, MH policies for post-1994 vintages have higher replacement costs and coverage amounts, and are more likely to be located in high-risk areas, all of which would tend to increase expected NFIP payments. These compositional shifts suggest that the estimated damage reductions comprise a lower bound on the true treatment effect of the HUD standard on flood damage.

Combining costs and benefits at the unit level yields a back-of-envelope private cost-benefit calculation for the purchaser of a post-1994 manufactured home. Among insured MH in the NFIP data, the pre-1994 annual claim rate is roughly `r claim_rate_fmt`. Applied to per-claim reductions of `r delta_bldg` in building damages and `r delta_cont` in contents damages, this implies an expected annual damage reduction of `r ann_benefit`, or `r npv_baseline` discounting at 3% over a 20-year MH lifespan. Expected savings from reduced flood damage alone are roughly `r bcr_pct` of the `r cost_fmt` price increase. Among the households who purchase flood insurance, the flood channel therefore recovers about a fifth of the cost, before counting the wind channel that the regulation actually targets, reduced displacement, or uninsured losses.

At the aggregate level, the reform generates meaningful fiscal spillovers. The point estimates imply reductions of roughly `r net_bldg_eff` in net building payments and `r net_cont_eff` in net contents payments per MH claim. Applied to the `r n_post_claims` claims on MH built between 1994 and 1999 observed in the NFIP sample, this yields roughly `r nfip_sav_m` in direct NFIP payment savings---a conservative figure that conditions on filing a claim and does not scale to the full stock of post-reform MH.[^fiscal-nfip] Spillovers to \emph{ex post} disaster relief---most notably FEMA Individual Assistance, SBA disaster loans, and state emergency grants---are likely substantially larger. <!--\textcolor{red}{[PLACEHOLDER: estimate of \emph{ex post} disaster relief spillover to be added.]}-->

[^fiscal-nfip]: The `r n_post_claims` claims for MH built 1994-1999 are observed over loss years 1994-2023. This calculation assumes no change in claim frequency or policy take-up and applies the main-specification payment reductions to the observed claim count.

This paper contributes to several literatures. First, it provides direct evidence on the returns to building code regulation for disaster resilience. @simmons_economic_2018 and @dehring_coastal_2013 study whether building code reforms in Florida for site-built homes improved resilience to hurricanes and find conflicting results. For manufactured housing, my results support a body of descriptive work examining the 1994 HUD code reform [@simmons_manufactured_2008; @kevin_r_grosskopf_manufactured_2005].

Methodologically, @baylis_mandated_2021 implement a similar study of wildfire building codes in California and find large benefits to mandatory adaptation, with fiscal spillovers and insurance value potentially justifying tighter building codes even in areas with moderate wildfire risk. This paper improves on their empirical strategy by exploiting the fact that manufactured homes are regulated federally, allowing me to disentangle building code reforms from general vintage effects. Specifically, I compare site-built and manufactured homes in the same area, exposed to the same floods, and built in the same year. My design builds on the set of methodologies used in the economics literature to study building codes, which generally rely on across-vintage or across-location comparisons [@jacobsen_are_2013; @levinson_how_2016]. My approach can be applied to any context where different housing types are subject to different regulatory bodies.

I also contribute to a rich literature evaluating the fiscal position of the National Flood Insurance Program and the broader fiscal consequences of natural disasters. My results suggest that HUD code reforms had moderate fiscal spillovers on the NFIP through reduced payouts on post-1994 MH claims, and likely larger spillovers on \emph{ex post} disaster relief programs that serve the largely uninsured MH population [@solomon_optimal_2026].

The scope of this paper is limited to only one channel of benefits -- flood damage reduction -- and does not attempt to estimate other benefits (e.g., wind damage reduction, spillovers to adjacent homes, reduced displacement, fiscal spillovers to \emph{ex post} disaster assistance). I leave the estimation of these channels to future work.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{institutional-background} describes the institutional background and the 1994 HUD Code reform. Section \ref{data} describes the data. Section \ref{empirical-strategy} presents the empirical strategy. Section \ref{results} reports the results, and Section \ref{conclusion} concludes.

# Institutional Background

## Manufactured Housing and the HUD Code

Approximately 6% of the housing stock are manufactured homes. This share is substantially higher in rural areas and in the Southeast, where the share of MH can exceed 15%.[^mh-stats] These homes are disproportionately occupied by low-income households, and they are disproportionately exposed to natural disaster risk. In 1992, Hurricane Andrew destroyed 97% of manufactured homes in its path in Dade County, Florida, compared to 11% of site-built homes.[^florida-case]

[^florida-case]: *Florida Manufactured Housing Ass'n v. Cisneros*, 53 F.3d 1565 (11th Cir. 1995).

[^mh-stats]: Manufactured-Housing Consumer Finance in the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 2014. https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/manufactured-housing-consumer-finance-in-the-u-s/. Manufactured homes are built in a factory and transported to a site, as distinct from site-built (stick-built) homes constructed on location.

The vulnerability of manufactured homes to extreme weather prompted a major regulatory response. In 1994, HUD revised the Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards---the federal building code governing all manufactured housing---to impose wind resistance requirements. The reform created a three-zone wind classification system and required structural upgrades for homes sited in high-wind zones, including stronger anchoring and strapping, upgraded sheathing and fastening schedules, and wind-pressure requirements for components and cladding. Unlike local building codes for site-built homes, the HUD Code is a federal minimum standard that preempts state and local regulation.

The preemption of local codes is a distinctive feature of the manufactured housing market. Site-built homes are subject to state and local building codes, which vary substantially across jurisdictions and are enforced through local permitting and inspection processes. Manufactured homes, by contrast, must meet a single federal standard. This institutional feature is central to the identification strategy: the 1994 reform was implemented through the federal HUD Code for manufactured homes, with wind-resistance requirements varying by HUD wind zone, while site-built homes remained governed by state and local codes. The reform was national in administration but not uniform in intensity---the binding upgrades applied to units sited in zones II and III---and the cost design in Section \ref{empirical-strategy} exploits exactly that differential exposure.

## NFIP and Flood Insurance for Manufactured Homes

The National Flood Insurance Program provides federally backed flood insurance to property owners in participating communities. Flood insurance is mandatory for properties with federally backed mortgages in FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs). The requirement turns on the lending channel and the covered security property rather than on the label attached to the financing. Manufactured homes are frequently financed with chattel loans (personal property loans secured by the home but not the land), many of which fall outside the federally regulated or federally connected lending that triggers mandatory purchase. Reduced exposure to the mandate is one reason NFIP take-up among manufactured homeowners is substantially lower than among site-built homeowners in comparable flood zones.

The NFIP data used in this paper record claims and policy information at the individual level. This allows direct comparison of flood damage outcomes between manufactured and site-built homes conditional on holding NFIP coverage. The selection into flood insurance coverage is a potential concern that I address through composition checks on the insured population in Section \ref{selection-and-composition}.

# Data

## Manufactured Housing Prices and Shipments

I estimate the price and quantity effects using a state-by-year panel from the Census Bureau's Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS), which reports average sales prices and placement counts by state. I focus on the period immediately around the HUD code change, 1988 - 1999. The treatment group consists of states containing HUD wind zones II or III; the control group is zone I states (see Figure \ref{map:treated-states}).

## Flood Damage and Insurance Coverage

I use two datasets from FEMA on individual flood insurance claims and policy records. Claims data record the date of loss, construction year, building and contents damage amounts, NFIP payments, property characteristics, and the census tract. Policy data record coverage amounts, premium, property characteristics, and flood zone designation. Both datasets include a field identifying manufactured homes.

### Final Sample

I restrict the sample to homes with construction years between 1983 and 1999 and loss dates from 1994 onward. Because claims for manufactured homes are relatively rare, I bin both the construction year and loss year in two and five year periods, respectively, to improve power.

For the policy analysis, I construct a balanced panel at the census tract $\times$ calendar-period $\times$ housing-type $\times$ construction-period level, which I aggregate to the county level for estimation. Policy records begin in 2009, so the policy panel spans the three five-year calendar periods 2009--2013, 2014--2018, and 2019--2023; claims are assigned to the same calendar periods, so a single period index serves both. Each cell reports the number of unique policies active at any time during the period along with the policy-weighted average of their characteristics. The panel is balanced over housing type and construction period within tract-periods that have positive policy exposure, so cells with zero claims but at least one active policy are retained and contribute a zero to the claim rate. Cells with zero active policies have no defined claim rate or average policy characteristics; they are dropped from the weighted cell-level regressions and enter only the Poisson count model of Section \ref{appendix-take-up}, where the outcome is the policy count itself.

All nominal values are deflated to constant (2000) dollars using the CPI-U. I restrict both samples to the continental US. Table \ref{tab:sumstats-nfip} reports summary statistics for the NFIP data by construction vintage and housing type. Manufactured homes generally experience lower building and contents damage than site-built homes, with correspondingly lower coverage amounts. I observe `r n_mh_claims` claims for manufactured homes in the sample, or roughly `r mh_claim_pct`% of all claims, substantially lower than the share of manufactured homes in the overall housing stock \citep{genz_why_2001}.

# Empirical Strategy

## Cost Estimation

I estimate the effect of the 1994 HUD standard on manufactured home prices using a two-way fixed effects event study:

\begin{equation}
\log(P_{st}) = \alpha_s + \gamma_t + \sum_{k \neq 1993} \beta_k (\mathbf{1}[\text{year} = k] \times \text{Treated}_s) + \varepsilon_{st}
\label{eq:event-study-cost}
\end{equation}

where $P_{st}$ is the average real sales price of manufactured homes in state $s$ in year $t$, $\alpha_s$ and $\gamma_t$ are state and year fixed effects, and $\text{Treated}_s$ indicates states containing wind zones II or III. The 1993 interaction is omitted: with state fixed effects the full set of treated-by-year interactions is collinear with the time-invariant treated indicator. The coefficients $\beta_k$ therefore trace out the price difference between treated and control states relative to 1993. Standard errors are clustered by state.

## Benefit Estimation: Event Study

The primary benefit-side specification is an event study that imposes no functional form on the vintage profile:

\begin{equation}
Y_{it} = \alpha_{c(i),t} + \delta_m + \lambda_{\nu_i} + \sum_{k \neq 1992} \beta_k (\mathbf{1}[\nu_i = k] \times \text{MH}_i) + \varepsilon_{it}
\label{eq:event-study-benefit}
\end{equation}

where $Y_{it}$ is the outcome for claim $i$ (e.g., building damage), $\alpha_{c(i),t}$ is a county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect absorbing location-specific storm severity, $\delta_m$ is a manufactured housing indicator absorbing time-invariant differences between housing types, $\text{MH}_i$ is an indicator for manufactured homes, and $\nu_i$ is the construction vintage bin of home $i$. The term $\lambda_{\nu_i}$ is a full set of construction-vintage fixed effects common to both housing types, so that the interactions are identified off deviations from the common vintage profile rather than off the level of that profile. The coefficients $\beta_k$ therefore capture the manufactured-home-specific vintage profile relative to the omitted 1992--1993 reference bin. Post-1994 coefficients are reduced-form cohort effects of exposure to the reform: because construction vintage is a proxy for actual regulatory exposure, the earliest post-reform bins are potentially attenuated by production-installation lags and incomplete compliance.

Identification relies on a parallel trends assumption in the vintage profile of outcomes between manufactured and site-built homes in the absence of the HUD code reform. In other words, homes built at different times may experience different levels of flood damage due to changes in construction quality, storm severity, or intra-county location, but these vintage effects should be the same for manufactured and site-built homes. I support this assumption by showing flat pre-trends in the event study specification across a broad range of claim-level and cell-level outcomes.

I expect the cohort effects to grow with later construction cohorts as compliance rates increase. Because of lags between production and installation, some units with post-1994 installation dates may have been manufactured before the regulation went into effect in July of 1994.

The cell-level specifications replace the county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect in Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-benefit} with a county $\times$ calendar-period fixed effect, since the cell panel is aggregated to five-year periods; regressions are weighted by the number of policies in the cell. The policy panel is described in Section \ref{data}.

# Results

## Cost Side: Manufactured Home Prices

Figure \ref{fig:es-price} presents the event study for manufactured home prices. Prior to 1994, treated and control states follow parallel trends: the pre-treatment coefficients are small, precisely estimated, and statistically indistinguishable from zero. Prices diverge sharply in 1994, with treated states experiencing a `r price_eff` increase that stabilizes by 1995 and persists through the end of the sample. The price effect is economically large, corresponding to an `r price_pct` increase in the price.

The 1994 break is consistent with prices adjusting around the July 1994 effective date. With annual price data the estimate cannot by itself distinguish anticipatory pricing from pass-through after implementation, since the 1994 coefficient mixes both halves of the year. The persistence of the premium through 2000 shows that the price gap was not a one-year implementation spike; its source---higher marginal production costs, fixed redesign costs amortized over many units, quality upgrading, or demand-side valuation of the improved construction---is not pinned down by the price path alone.

Figure \ref{fig:es-placements} shows the corresponding event study for log placements. The point estimates are small, centered around zero, and statistically insignificant throughout the post-period, so the data do not show a large decline in the quantity of manufactured homes shipped to treated states. The estimates are imprecise enough that a modest decline would be difficult to detect, and they are consistent with a small decline in placements, with relatively inelastic demand, or with an outward demand shift from the improved construction offsetting the higher price.

## Benefit Side: Flood Damage

### Post 1994 MH experience lower flood damages

Figure \ref{fig:es-building-damage} presents the event study for building damage per claim. Pre-1994 construction-period coefficients are flat and close to zero, confirming parallel vintage trends between manufactured and site-built homes before the HUD standard took effect. Beginning with the 1994 construction cohort, manufactured homes experience sharply lower building damage relative to site-built homes, stabilizing at over `r bldg_dmg_evt_avg` per claim in later cohorts as compliance ramps up. Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes-static} collapses this vintage profile to a single pre/post-1994 comparison: manufactured homes built after 1994 experience `r bldg_dmg_eff` (SE `r bldg_dmg_se`) lower building damage per claim than site-built homes of the same vintage, or almost `r bldg_pct_avg`% of the average building damage across all claims. I report this static estimate as the headline number, since it is a single precisely-estimated average treatment effect rather than an average of eleven individually-noisy event-study coefficients; the event study itself remains the vehicle for showing flat pre-trends and the compliance ramp.

Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes} presents supplementary outcomes on insurance payments and damage to the building's contents. Column (3) shows effects on building damage as a share of its assessed value, measured in percent. Conditional on filing a claim, post-1994 manufactured homes experience damage that is `r bldg_shr_static` percentage points (SE `r bldg_shr_static_se`) lower as a share of assessed value than site-built homes of the same vintage, taking the static estimate in column (3) of Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes-static}. This is a percentage-point change in the damage-to-value ratio, not a percent change in damage; against the mean share reported at the foot of the table it is a large proportional decline. While the HUD wind standard raised prices, it decreased both absolute and relative flood damages. Contents damage and payments decline by roughly `r cont_dmg_eff` and `r net_cont_eff`, respectively, consistent with improved structural integrity.

## Selection and Composition {#selection-and-composition}

A concern with the vintage-based design is that post-1994 manufactured home policyholders may differ systematically from pre-1994 policyholders, and that these compositional differences rather than construction quality drive the damage results. Table \ref{tab:composition} reports the full set of policy composition event studies.

The composition shifts work against the main result. Relative to pre-1994 manufactured homes, post-1994 manufactured home policies have higher replacement cost (\$20--30,000), higher building coverage (\$8--15,000 per policy), and higher contents coverage (\$1--2,000 per policy). Post-1994 manufactured homes are also more concentrated in SFHAs (3--7 percentage points higher). These shifts would all tend to increase expected NFIP payments, not lower them, making the damage reduction estimates conservative.

The one composition shift that works in the direction of the main result is the elevated-building share, which rises only for the latest construction vintages in the sample. Its timing matters: because the increase appears well after 1994, elevation cannot account for the damage reductions estimated in the 1994--1996 bins, and it can bear on the interpretation only of the later cohorts. For those cohorts elevation is plausibly part of the treatment channel---the HUD Code encouraged improved siting and installation practices---rather than a confound. Primary-residence share and mandatory purchases are essentially unchanged across vintages.

# Discussion

## Cost-Benefit

The cost and benefit estimates can be combined in a back-of-envelope calculation. The per-unit compliance cost is approximately `r cost_fmt`, paid once at purchase. The per-event reduction is roughly `r delta_bldg` in building damage and `r delta_cont` in contents damage, for a total of `r delta_total` per flood event.

The expected benefit depends on the probability of experiencing a flood. Among manufactured homes in the NFIP data, the baseline claim rate is approximately `r round(get_welf("claim_rate_pooled_pre"), 3)` claims per year, yielding an expected annual damage reduction of `r ann_benefit`. Discounting at 3% over a 20-year lifespan yields an expected present value of roughly `r npv_baseline` in flood damage reduction.

Several factors suggest that these benefits are a lower bound on the total private return. First, the HUD standard targeted wind resilience, not flood protection, but NFIP claims are triggered only by flood events. The flood damage reductions estimated here are therefore only part of the full resilience benefits. Second, damage to buildings and contents represents only one part of losses related to climate disasters, which also include displacement costs, lost income, and other indirect costs. Finally, risk-averse households may value the insurance value of greater protection against climate damages.

However, private benefits may be overstated if households select into NFIP based on their flood risk. Standard adverse selection would imply that insured MH face higher flood exposure than the average MH, so the claim rate of `r claim_rate_fmt` would overstate the hazard a typical MH confronts and the extrapolated benefit would be too high. Conversely, take-up of NFIP coverage is correlated with income, and low-income MH residents---who are less likely to purchase---may occupy lower-quality sites with greater flood exposure, implying the opposite sign of selection [@landry_flood_2011].

Social returns may be yet greater for two reasons. First, the code change caused fiscal spillovers on FEMA via both changes in NFIP payments and FEMA's \emph{ex post} disaster relief, predominantly provided through its Individual Assistance program. Reduced damage to post-1994 manufactured homes reduces these federal outlays, though I do not estimate effects on ex post relief directly.[^fiscal-spillover]

[^fiscal-spillover]: \cite{solomon_optimal_2026} study how changes in insurance take-up (rather than damages) affect relief spending. In principle, FEMA's individual assistance relief does not cover towards insured losses, and they find this borne in the data: an additional 1% of houses that are insured lowers ex post government spending by $175-$203 per house-flood.

# Conclusion

The 1994 HUD wind standard reform raised manufactured home prices by roughly `r price_eff`. Among NFIP-insured claimants, post-1994 manufactured homes experience about `r delta_bldg` lower building damage and about `r delta_cont` lower contents damage per claim, or `r delta_total` in total per flood event. Applying the pre-reform claim rate and discounting at 3% over a 20-year lifespan, those per-claim reductions imply roughly `r npv_baseline` in expected present-value flood benefits---about `r bcr_pct` of the price increase.

For the 22 million Americans living in manufactured homes---disproportionately low-income, credit-constrained, and underinsured---these findings have policy relevance, with one boundary worth drawing clearly. Because the HUD standard applies at construction, it may provide protection even for households that private insurance markets do not reach; but the estimates in this paper are measured among NFIP-insured claimants, who are likely more selected and more financially connected than the uninsured manufactured-home population the framing highlights. Subject to that caveat, the results suggest that building code reform can generate meaningful disaster-loss reductions, and that the full return may be larger once wind losses, uninsured losses, displacement costs, risk aversion, and fiscal spillovers are accounted for. As climate change intensifies hurricane and flood risk, the returns to mandated adaptation investment in this housing sector are likely growing.

\appendix

# NFIP Take-Up {#appendix-take-up}

The damage estimates in the main text condition on filing a claim and do not speak to whether the HUD code reform affected NFIP take-up. In standard models, self-protection can reduce the private value of insurance when coverage is costly, so the reform could in principle lower voluntary NFIP demand \citep{ehrlich_market_1972}. The sign is not general: it depends on premium loading, mandatory purchase rules, borrowing constraints, and basis risk, and under actuarially fair full insurance a lower loss probability does not by itself imply lower optimal coverage. This appendix examines whether the reform affected the rate at which manufactured homeowners hold NFIP policies and file claims, relative to the stock of homes of that vintage and type -- not just the raw count of policies, which mechanically tracks how many homes of a given vintage exist.

The raw policy count is not interpretable as a take-up rate on its own, since it moves with both take-up and the underlying number of homes of that vintage. An earlier version of this table divided policy counts by county single-family building-permit counts, but that denominator is the wrong housing type (permits for site-built construction, applied to manufactured and site-built rows alike) and undercounts non-randomly: median BPS coverage of the site-built stock falls from 0.70 in low-MH counties to 0.20 in high-MH counties, exactly where manufactured housing concentrates. I instead construct `homes_n`, an imputed stock of homes by county, construction year, and housing type. Levels come from the 2000 Census, which counts a mobile home as a housing unit regardless of titling, so there is no chattel-titling gap; within a Census vintage bin, the annual split uses Survey of Manufactured Housing state-year placements (for MH) and BPS county-year single-family permits, falling back to the state permit share where a county reports none (for site-built homes). These annual sources are used only to divide a Census-anchored bin total across years, so their own level bias cancels out of the ratio; construction year 1994 itself is dropped from the imputation as an ambiguous mix of pre- and post-reform units, given the code's July effective date and production/installation lags.

Table \ref{tab:take-up} reports OLS estimates of `policies_per_1k_homes` and `claims_per_1k_homes` directly, weighted by `homes_n` (a handful of cells have imputed stock well under one home, mostly in the already-flagged 1994 construction-year bin, and would otherwise dominate an unweighted fit) and clustered by county, pooling all three policy periods (2009-2023). An earliest-period-only (2009-2013) restriction, meant to limit exposure to differential attrition of the stock between the 2000 Census and the policy data, was checked and dropped from the table: its point estimates were extremely similar to the pooled column and added no information. The pooled post-1994 average coefficient is `r ppl_home_per1k` policies and `r clm_home_per1k` claims per 1,000 homes, both relative to site-built homes of the same vintage -- small in magnitude and, unlike the raw policy count, not mechanically explained by more manufactured homes existing in later cohorts. The 1994 vintage bin (built from a single, ambiguous construction year rather than the full two-year bin -- see the stock-construction note above) is the most volatile point in every specification and drives most of the pooled average; the 1996 and 1998 bins are small and closer to zero. I read this as no clear evidence of a first-order shift in take-up or claim frequency at the extensive margin, in contrast to the sizable damage-severity effect in the main text. This decomposes the benefit side into two margins with different welfare interpretations: the claims-per-home (extensive/insurability) margin reported here, and the payment-conditional-on-a-claim (intensive) margin reported in the main damage-outcome tables, which does not require this stock denominator at all.

  \centering
  \caption{NFIP Take-Up per Housing-Unit Stock}\label{tab:take-up}
  \begin{threeparttable}
    \input{output/event-study/countyfp/take-up.tex}
    \begin{tablenotes}
      \item Notes: OLS models of policies (or claims) per 1,000 homes, weighted by $\mathrm{homes\_n}$ (an imputed county $\times$ construction-year $\times$ housing-type stock of homes, see text) and clustered by county. The policy panel is indexed by county, calendar period (five-year bins covering 2009--2023), housing type, and construction-vintage bin; the specification replaces the county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect in Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-benefit} with a county $\times$ calendar-period fixed effect and retains the common vintage and housing-type fixed effects. Source: OpenFEMA policy data; Census 2000; Survey of Manufactured Housing; Census Building Permits Survey.
    \end{tablenotes}
  \end{threeparttable}

**Caveat: the stock denominator is a 2000 snapshot, the policy data are not.** `homes_n` is fixed as of the 2000 Census, while the policy periods run from 2009 to 2023 -- 9 to 23 years later. If pre- and post-1994 manufactured homes attrite (are demolished, relocated, or converted) at different rates over that gap, the true denominator drifts away from the Census-fixed one asymmetrically by vintage, and the bias grows with the gap. An earlier version of this table reported the 2009--2013 calendar period separately, as the closest snapshot to 2000 and so the least exposed to this drift; its point estimates were extremely similar to the pooled 2009--2023 column, so it was dropped from the table without evidence that attrition is materially distorting the pooled estimate. The ACS's continuously updated housing-vintage tables could in principle bound the drift directly, but cannot substitute for `homes_n`: ACS year-built categories are decade bins that cannot isolate 1994 even in principle, and tract-level manufactured-home counts carry very large margins of error. Bounding the 2014--2023 estimates against the ACS decade series is left for future work.

# Wind-Zone Treatment Intensity by State {#appendix-windzone-intensity}

The binary treatment indicator used in the main cost-side specification (Table \ref{tab:mhs-dose-response}, column 1) codes a state as treated if it contains any Zone II or III county, regardless of how much of the state's manufactured housing stock actually sits in one. This is a coarse proxy: a state can be classified treated on the strength of a single high-wind county while the bulk of its MH stock sits in Zone I. Table \ref{tab:windzone-intensity} reports, for every state with at least one Zone II/III county, the share of its 1980--2000 manufactured-housing stock located in a Zone II/III county, constructed by weighting each county's wind-zone status (24 CFR \S 3280.305, as classified in the eCFR crosswalk) by its manufactured-housing stock from the 2000 Census. Only 3 of the 11 treated states---Florida, Louisiana, and Massachusetts---have more than half of their MH stock in a Zone II/III county; pooling across all treated states, only about 30\% of the 1980--2000 MH stock sits in a Zone II/III county. This intensity measure underlies the continuous-treatment column of Table \ref{tab:mhs-dose-response}.
